section.title: Benjamin's Allotment
section.sectionRationale: The nation gathers at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting, and Joshua confronts the seven tribes who have not yet taken their inheritance: how long will you put off possessing the land the LORD has given you? The land is surveyed, divided into seven portions, and distributed by lot before the LORD, beginning with Benjamin. It is one movement, the renewed distribution at Shiloh, which rebukes spiritual slackness and calls God's people to actively enter what He has freely given.
section.thesis: God has given the land, yet seven tribes hang back from possessing it, so Joshua rebukes their delay and organizes a careful, worshipful distribution by lot at the sanctuary, teaching that the sure gift of God is not to be neglected but entered, and Benjamin, small but strategically placed, receives its portion first.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the assembly at Shiloh and Joshua's rebuke of delay, verses 1 to 7; the survey and casting of lots before the LORD, verses 8 to 10; and Benjamin's borders and cities, verses 11 to 28.

units.label: The assembly at Shiloh and Joshua's rebuke
units.note: how long will you put off possessing the land

verses.text: Then the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there. And though the land was subdued before them,
there were still seven tribes of Israel who had not yet received their inheritance.
So Joshua said to the Israelites, “How long will you {{rafah|put off}} entering and possessing the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?
Appoint three men from each tribe, and I will send them out to survey the land and map it out, according to the inheritance of each. Then they will return to me
and divide the land into seven portions. Judah shall remain in their territory in the south, and the house of Joseph shall remain in their territory in the north.
When you have mapped out the seven portions of land and brought it to me, I will cast {{goral|lots}} for you here in the presence of the LORD our God.

The Levites, however, have no portion among you, because their inheritance is the priesthood of the LORD. And Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh have already received the inheritance that Moses the servant of the LORD gave them beyond the Jordan to the east.”

units.label: The survey and casting of lots before the LORD
units.note: Joshua cast lots in the presence of the LORD at Shiloh

verses.text: As the men got up to go out, Joshua commanded them to map out the land, saying, “Go and survey the land, map it out, and return to me. Then I will cast lots for you here in Shiloh in the presence of the LORD.”
So the men departed and went throughout the land, mapping it city by city into seven portions. Then they returned with the document to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh.
And Joshua cast lots for them in the presence of the LORD at Shiloh, where he distributed the land to the Israelites according to their divisions.

units.label: Benjamin's borders and cities
units.note: the first lot came up for Benjamin

verses.text: The first lot came up for the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. Their allotted territory lay between the tribes of Judah and Joseph:
On the north side their border began at the Jordan, went up past the northern slope of Jericho, headed west through the hill country, and came out at the wilderness of Beth-aven.
From there the border crossed over to the southern slope of Luz (that is, Bethel) and went down to Ataroth-addar on the hill south of Lower Beth-horon.

On the west side the border curved southward from the hill facing Beth-horon on the south and came out at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city of the sons of Judah. This was the western side.
On the south side the border began at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim and extended westward to the spring at the Waters of Nephtoah.

Then it went down to the foot of the hill that faces the Valley of Ben-hinnom at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim and ran down the Valley of Hinnom toward the southern slope of the Jebusites and downward to En-rogel.
From there it curved northward and proceeded to En-shemesh and on to Geliloth facing the Ascent of Adummim, and continued down to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben.
Then it went on to the northern slope of Beth-arabah and went down into the valley.
The border continued to the northern slope of Beth-hoglah and came out at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the mouth of the Jordan. This was the southern border.
On the east side the border was the Jordan. These were the borders around the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin.
These were the cities of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin: Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz,
Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel,
Avvim, Parah, Ophrah,
Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba, twelve cities, along with their villages.
Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth,
Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,
Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,
Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah, and Kiriath-jearim, fourteen cities, along with their villages. This was the {{nachalah|inheritance}} of the clans of the tribe of Benjamin.

rafah.gloss: To be slack, to sink down, to let drop, to be lax. Joshua asks how long the tribes will rafah, be slack about entering and possessing the land. The word rebukes a spiritual laziness that hangs back from claiming what God has already given; the gift is sure, but it must be actively laid hold of, not neglected through complacency and delay.

goral.gloss: A lot, cast to seek God's decision. The remaining land is divided by goral in the presence of the LORD at Shiloh, so each portion is received as God's own assignment rather than human choice. Casting lots before the sanctuary joins the practical work of distribution to worship, submitting the outcome to the LORD, Proverbs 16:33.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession. Benjamin's nachalah, small but wedged strategically between Judah and Joseph and holding sites like Bethel, Gibeon, and the border of Jerusalem, is received by lot as God's gift. The chapter presses that such an inheritance, freely given, is meant to be entered and possessed, not left idle.

basic.context: The nation gathers at Shiloh, and for the first time the Tent of Meeting, the center of Israel's worship, is set up in the land. But even though the land has been subdued, seven tribes still have not taken their inheritance. Joshua confronts them with a pointed question: how long will you put off possessing the land the LORD has given you? He organizes a solution: survey the remaining land, divide it into seven portions, and distribute it by lot before the LORD. The lot falls first to Benjamin, a small tribe placed strategically between Judah and Joseph, holding key sites and the border of Jerusalem. The question underneath is: why would God's people hesitate to take hold of a gift He has freely given, and what does it mean to enter fully into what is ours?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative combining a rebuke, a process of distribution, and a land record. The key spiritual point is Joshua's question about delay: the gift is sure, but it must be possessed. This becomes a rich picture of the Christian life, where believers are called to lay hold of what God has already secured for them. The setting up of the Tent of Meeting at Shiloh also marks the centrality of worship in the settled land.
basic.originalLanguages: Joshua rebukes the tribes for being rafah, slack, in possessing the land. The distribution is done by goral, by lot, before the LORD. And Benjamin receives its nachalah, its inheritance, small but strategically placed.
basic.typology: The call not to be slack but to possess what God has given pictures the believer's call to lay hold of the inheritance secured in Christ. The Tent of Meeting set up at Shiloh, God dwelling among His settled people, points to God dwelling with His people in Christ and finally in the new creation.
basic.christ: The land was given yet had to be possessed, a pattern fulfilled in Christ, who has secured every spiritual blessing for His people, which they are then called to lay hold of by faith. And the Tent of Meeting at the center of the nation points to God dwelling among His people, fulfilled in Christ, the Word who tabernacled among us, and in the church as God's dwelling by the Spirit.
basic.god: God is the generous giver who has already granted the land; the delay is the people's fault, not His. He is the God who is to be worshiped at the center of national life, His Tent of Meeting pitched at Shiloh. And He is the sovereign who assigns each portion by lot, so that the inheritance is His gift and His arrangement.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 4 warns against failing to enter God's rest through unbelief. Ephesians 1 speaks of the spiritual inheritance secured in Christ. John 1 says the Word tabernacled among us. And Philippians 3 urges pressing on to lay hold of that for which Christ laid hold of us.
basic.oneStory: At Shiloh, with the Tent of Meeting at the center, Joshua rebukes the tribes' slackness and organizes the distribution of the remaining land by lot before the LORD. The call to possess the sure gift, and the presence of God at the center of the people, point forward to Christ, in whom the inheritance is secured and God dwells among His people.

context.literary: Chapter 18 marks a hinge in the whole allotment section. Judah and the house of Joseph had already received their land in chapters 15 to 17 through direct assignment; here the process changes to survey first, then lot, for the seven tribes still waiting, and Joshua explicitly tells the surveyors that Judah shall remain in their territory in the south and the house of Joseph shall remain in theirs in the north, verse 5, so the new method works around what is already fixed rather than reopening it. The rebuke of verses 1 to 3 uses the stock idiom of impatience found elsewhere in Scripture whenever God's patience with delay is wearing thin, the same how long that Moses hears at the manna and the spies, and that later prophets and psalmists fling back at God Himself. Structurally, this chapter opens a frame that the whole remaining allotment will close: it begins with the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh, verse 1, and the seven-chapter unit will end with almost the identical formula, at Shiloh before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, 19:51, so Benjamin's long, seemingly ordinary list of borders and towns in verses 11 to 28 sits inside a carefully bracketed unit that both opens and closes as an act of worship rather than mere administration.
context.historical: Shiloh lay roughly at the geographic center of the tribal territories in the hill country of Ephraim, reachable from every direction, which is likely why it, rather than Gilgal where the nation had camped through the conquest, became the settled home of the Tent of Meeting from this point until the ark was captured in the days of Eli, generations later. Counting carefully explains the seven tribes of verse 2: of the twelve, Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh had already settled east of the Jordan under Moses, and Judah, Ephraim, and the other half of Manasseh had just received their land in the west, leaving Benjamin, Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan still to be placed. Benjamin's own portion turned out to be a narrow wedge squeezed between the two largest allotments, Judah to the south and Joseph to the north, yet it held an outsized share of significant towns for so small a strip of hill country, including Jericho at its eastern edge, Bethel and Gibeon toward the center, and the disputed border town of Jebus at its southern tip, a location whose small size would later prove no barrier to real influence in Israel's story.
context.canonical: Two of the towns simply listed here in verse 25 and verse 28 carry weight far beyond this chapter. Gibeon, spared by the oath Israel swore to its inhabitants in chapter 9 rather than taken by the sword, turns up quietly folded into Benjamin's ordinary city list, its earlier, dramatic story now settled into the routine business of tribal geography. Gibeah, listed here as nothing more than one Benjamite town among many, becomes a few generations later the scene of the outrage that very nearly erases Benjamin from Israel altogether, when the tribes unite in horror and near-annihilation against their own kinsmen, Judges 19 to 21, a stark reminder that receiving an inheritance in peace is no guarantee that peace will last. And Jebus, named here as Benjamin's, that is, Jerusalem, verse 28, sits on a border no single tribe would ever cleanly own; Judah's list in chapter 15 had already claimed its southern edge, and it would take David, uniting both a southern and a northern tribe's ancestral claims, to finally take the whole city and make it fit to be every tribe's capital, 2 Samuel 5:6-9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer wants the reader to feel the awkwardness of the opening scene: the land lies subdued, the fighting is essentially over, and still seven whole tribes are camping rather than settling. Rather than simply recording that awkwardness, Joshua turns it into pointed speech, asking a question that expects an answer and a change of behavior, not just information. The choice to hand the actual legwork to three men from each tribe, rather than have Joshua himself walk the whole country, shows a leader delegating real responsibility once he has supplied the necessary push, and the survey's return as a written document, read and then divided by lot before the LORD, models a process where human diligence and divine decision are not rivals but partners. By placing Benjamin's exhaustive city list right after this rebuke and process, the author lets the sheer detail of the resulting record answer the opening question: this is what it looks like when a people stop delaying and let the process run to completion, town by town, all the way to twenty-six named cities for one small tribe.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The mechanics of surveying and casting lots belonged to a specific moment in Israel's covenant life and are not a repeatable method for believers today, who are not told to divide up decisions by lot; the last time Scripture records the practice for a major decision is the choosing of Matthias in Acts 1:26, before the Spirit is given at Pentecost, after which guidance comes by other, more direct means. What does transfer is the pattern behind the practice: fair, transparent process joined to conscious dependence on God rather than on tribal leverage or self-assertion. Likewise, Joshua's rebuke is not a timeless command to hurry every task, but it does press a durable principle, that a real gift already granted can still sit unclaimed through nothing but inertia, and that leaders bear real responsibility to name that inertia plainly rather than let it drift on unaddressed.

debates.question: Why did seven tribes delay in taking their inheritance?

views.label: Spiritual slackness and complacency
views.case: Joshua's word, how long will you put off, uses the language of slackness, suggesting a laziness or loss of resolve; with the land largely subdued, the urgency had faded, and the tribes grew content to camp rather than do the work of surveying, claiming, and settling their portions, a complacency Joshua rebukes.

views.label: Reluctance to face the remaining hard work of possession
views.case: Taking full possession meant driving out remaining Canaanites and settling difficult territory; the tribes may have shrunk from that effort, preferring the security of the camp, so their delay reflects the same reluctance to trust God for the hard parts of the conquest seen in the tribes of Joseph.

debates.bearing: Either way, Joshua treats the delay as a failure to lay hold of God's sure gift, a warning against neglecting or drifting from what God has freely given rather than actively entering it.

debates.question: Was casting lots here a mechanical act of chance, a mystical oracle, or something else?

views.label: An act of prayerful submission before God
views.case: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD, Proverbs 16:33, and the chapter twice specifies that this lot fell in the presence of the LORD at Shiloh, verses 6 and 10, so the outcome, whatever the mechanism, was received as His own determination rather than random luck, an act of worship rather than a coin toss.

views.label: A practical, fair method layered under a prior human survey
views.case: The land had already been walked, measured, and divided into seven comparable portions by the tribal representatives before any lot was cast, verse 9, so the lot's real function was simply to assign which already-equalized portion went to which tribe, removing any appearance of favoritism between tribes of different size and standing rather than dictating every boundary directly.

debates.bearing: The chapter does not force a choice between the two: careful human survey did the practical work of dividing the land fairly, while the lot, cast before the LORD, entrusted the assignment itself to His decision rather than to protest or preference, joining fairness and faith without reducing either to mere superstition.

study.originalLanguages: Four words carry the chapter's argument beyond the ones already named. The whole body gathered at Shiloh is called the edah, the congregation, a term used across the Torah for Israel formally assembled under covenant rather than merely present in one place; the same word describes Israel gathered at Sinai and gathered for judgment in the wilderness, so its use here signals that this is not a casual camp meeting but the covenant nation convened as one body to finish covenant business. Joshua's rebuke opens with ad anah, how long, a fixed idiom of exasperated patience that recurs across Scripture whenever God or His spokesman presses a people who are dragging their feet, the same phrase behind Moses' complaint about the people's grumbling and behind the psalmist's own cry, how long, O LORD, will You forget me, Psalm 13:1; hearing it here casts Joshua's question less as mild encouragement and more as a leader naming a pattern of delay he recognizes and will not let stand. The survey itself is handled in the language of documentation: the men map the land and bring back a sefer, a written scroll or document, verse 9, the ordinary word elsewhere used for the scroll of the law itself, so that Israel's inheritance, like Israel's covenant, ends up fixed in writing rather than left to memory or dispute. And the portions themselves are repeatedly a cheleq, a share or allotted part, from the same root as the verb to divide used through this section; every tribe receives not a vague region but a chelek, a defined share carved out of one whole, so that the language of division throughout insists the land was one gift being fairly apportioned rather than separate prizes being separately won. One more thread is worth naming. The chapter's repeated formula, this was the inheritance of the clans, uses mishpachah, clan or family group, the same word structuring nearly every tribal census in Numbers; boundaries here are never drawn around individuals but around extended kin groups, so that Benjamin's land is really a patchwork of family shares held together under one tribal name, a reminder that Israel's inheritance was always a web of households before it was a line on any map.

typology.type: Gibeon, spared by covenant oath in chapter 9, folded quietly into Benjamin's ordinary list of towns, 18:25
typology.fulfillment: A people once outside Israel by birth, admitted only by a solemn pledge rather than by conquest, end up simply living inside the tribal boundary being drawn here, no longer a special case requiring explanation. It pictures how those once far off and outside the commonwealth of Israel are brought near and made fellow citizens with the saints, members of the same household, no longer strangers needing a separate story, Ephesians 2:12-13 and 2:19.

typology.type: The lot cast in the presence of the LORD to settle what human survey alone could not decide, 18:6 and 10
typology.fulfillment: Human process reaches its limit and the outcome is entrusted to God's own determination rather than to negotiation. The pattern anticipates the one casting of lots that mattered most of all, when soldiers at the cross divided Christ's garments among themselves by lot, unknowingly fulfilling a Scripture written centuries before, Psalm 22:18 and John 19:23-24, human chance again serving, without knowing it, a sovereign and long-written purpose.

typology.type: Jerusalem sitting exactly on Benjamin's southern border, claimed by no tribe's clean and undisputed possession, 18:28
typology.fulfillment: A city too significant to belong cleanly to one tribe, needing a king who could unite two ancestral claims before it was truly taken, anticipates a city that will not finally belong to one nation either, but will come down from God as the shared dwelling place of every people, the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:2-3 and 21:24. What Benjamin and Judah could only hold jointly and uneasily on a shared border, that final city will hold openly, its gates never shut, because the nations once kept outside are welcomed all the way in rather than merely tolerated at the edge.

study.christ: One detail in this chapter is easy to read past and hard to forget once noticed: the sanctuary that is now set up permanently sits in a town called Shiloh, and that exact word appears in one of the most debated lines in all of Genesis, Jacob's blessing over Judah, that the scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, Genesis 49:10. Hebrew readers have long argued over whether that word names a coming person, a place, or reads slightly differently in the oldest manuscripts, and no firm claim should be built on the coincidence alone. But it is a striking coincidence: Israel's tent of worship comes to rest, seemingly by ordinary geography, in a town that carries the very name Jacob had once tied to Judah's future king. The chapter's other pointer to Christ is more certain. When the surveyed land could not be fairly divided by argument or negotiation, Israel cast lots before the LORD and trusted the result as His own, and centuries later soldiers who had no interest in Scripture at all cast lots for Christ's clothing at the foot of the cross, doing exactly what an old psalm had already described, they divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing, Psalm 22:18, fulfilled in John 19:23-24. What looked like chance both at Shiloh and at Calvary was, in fact, obedience to a will fixed long before either scene played out. And Benjamin's own inheritance, wedged between Judah and Joseph and including a city, Jerusalem, that belonged fully to neither, points toward the son of David who would one day rule from exactly that contested ground, a king from Judah's tribe reigning over a city that had needed both a southern and a northern tribe's claim to become one capital, a small foreshadowing of the greater King who gathers what no single tribe or nation could unite on its own, Ephesians 2:14-16.
study.god: Read closely, this chapter shows a God who works through ordinary process and holy decision at the very same time without letting either one crowd out the other. Three men per tribe walk the land on foot and write down what they find; nothing here is mystical or hidden, it is careful, plain fieldwork. Yet the phrase in the presence of the LORD is repeated three times in ten verses, at the promise of the survey, at its instruction, and at the casting itself, so that this most mundane of tasks, drawing lines on a map, is treated the entire time as something done under God's eye rather than merely among men. He is also strikingly patient and strikingly impatient in the same breath: patient enough that seven tribes had been allowed to camp for some time without immediate correction, yet not endlessly patient, since He presses His question through Joshua the moment that delay threatens to become permanent default. And He is even handed in a way the record itself displays rather than states: a small, squeezed tribe like Benjamin, wedged into a narrow strip between two much larger neighbors, receives exactly the same careful boundary description, town by town, that Judah's far larger territory received in chapter 15, so that no tribe's smallness becomes an excuse for a thinner account of what God gave it. This is a God who does not ration His attention according to a people's size or prominence, and who folds the plainest administrative work of a settling nation into an act done, quite literally, before His own face. This same God is unhurried about the order in which He acts even while He is exacting about the outcome. Judah and Joseph are settled first and simply told to stay where they are; the remaining seven wait through an entire process of survey and lot before Benjamin's turn even arrives in the text, yet nothing about that wait suggests neglect, since the very care lavished on this small tribe's boundary, verse by verse, shows a God who was never in a hurry to shortchange the last in line for the sake of the first.

crossReferences.note: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD, the principle behind Joshua's careful insistence that Benjamin and the other six tribes receive their portions by lot in the presence of the LORD rather than by human negotiation.

The apostles cast lots to choose Matthias, the last such instance recorded in Scripture, before the Spirit is given at Pentecost; the practice of Joshua 18 belongs to a specific covenant moment rather than an ongoing pattern for guidance today.

Gibeon is spared by Israel's sworn oath rather than conquered by the sword; its quiet appearance among Benjamin's cities in this chapter shows a former enemy fully settled within Israel's own tribal boundary.
Gibeah, listed here as an unremarkable Benjamite town, becomes a generation later the scene of an outrage so severe it nearly destroys the tribe of Benjamin entirely in the civil war that follows.

Jerusalem, straddling Benjamin's southern border here, is not fully secured for Israel until David takes the Jebusite stronghold and makes it his capital, uniting a claim no single tribe had managed alone.

Jacob's blessing ties Judah's future ruler to a word, Shiloh, that is also the very name of the town where the Tent of Meeting now permanently stands, a debated but striking overlap between this chapter's setting and Judah's messianic promise.
They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing, written centuries before the cross, gives the lot cast before the LORD in this chapter its deepest later echo.

Christ Himself is our peace, uniting two into one and breaking down the dividing wall of hostility, the reality that Benjamin's own contested border city, Jerusalem, would only foreshadow once a king from Judah finally united it.

study.oneStory: The conquest chapters that open this book move at speed, city after city falling in a handful of campaigns; the settlement chapters that follow move at the pace of paperwork, and chapter 18 is the moment the narrative openly admits that gap in pace has become a problem. Seven tribes are still camping when the fighting is essentially finished, and the story pauses long enough for its hero to ask the question every reader of Israel's later history will eventually ask on the nation's behalf: how long will you put off entering what has already been given? The answer here is a good one, a fair survey, a written record, a lot cast before the LORD, and Benjamin, the smallest and most hemmed in of the seven, receiving as full and careful an account of its towns as any larger tribe. But the same soil that receives this careful, worshipful attention will not stay unspoiled. Gibeon's old story of mercy and Gibeah's coming story of outrage are already folded into this single tribe's list of towns, a sign that inheriting land in peace never guarantees keeping it in holiness. The generations after Joshua will need judges, then a king from this very tribe who fails, then a king from Judah who succeeds where Benjamin's own son could not, and finally a city on Benjamin's own border that neither tribe alone can secure until David unites what Joshua's lot had merely placed side by side. The whole trajectory bends toward a greater King who does not need a lot cast to determine His inheritance, since the nations themselves are already given Him as His possession, and toward a city, a new Jerusalem, that will not sit on any one tribe's border but will come down as the dwelling of God with every people, the last and lasting answer to a chapter that began with a nation still camping outside what was already theirs.

quiz.q: What did Joshua rebuke the seven tribes for?

options.text: For being slow to enter and possess the land the LORD had already given them.
options.note: Verse 3 records Joshua's rebuke of their delay in possessing the inheritance.

options.text: For fighting each other over the best land.
options.note: The issue was not infighting but their slackness in possessing what God had given.

options.text: For worshiping the gods of the Canaanites.
options.note: Idolatry is not the charge here; the rebuke is for delay in taking their inheritance.

options.text: For refusing to help the eastern tribes.
options.note: The eastern tribes already had their land; the rebuke concerns the seven tribes' own delay.

quiz.q: How was the remaining land distributed?

options.text: It was surveyed, divided into seven portions, and assigned by lot before the LORD at Shiloh.
options.note: Verses 4 to 10 describe the survey and casting of lots in God's presence.

options.text: Joshua simply handed each tribe whatever it asked for.
options.note: The land was carefully surveyed and assigned by lot, not given on request.

options.text: The tribes seized whatever land they could hold.
options.note: The distribution was orderly, by lot before the LORD, not a seizure.

options.text: The land was sold to the highest bidders.
options.note: It was assigned by lot as God's gift, not sold.

quiz.q: What significant thing was set up at Shiloh?

options.text: The Tent of Meeting, Israel's center of worship, now placed in the heart of the land.
options.note: Verse 1 marks the establishment of the Tent of Meeting at Shiloh.

options.text: A new fortress to defend against the Philistines.
options.note: Shiloh became a worship center, not a military fortress.
Joshua was no king with a palace; what was set up was the Tent of Meeting for worship.

options.text: A marketplace for trade among the tribes.
options.note: What was established was the sanctuary, the Tent of Meeting, not a marketplace.

quiz.q: What lasting lesson does Joshua's rebuke teach?

options.text: God's people should not be slack but actively lay hold of what He has freely given.
options.note: The gift was sure; the call was to possess it, a pattern the New Testament applies to entering God's rest.

options.text: God's gifts must always be earned by hard labor first.
options.note: The land was a gift already given; the point is possessing it by faith, not earning it.

options.text: It is fine to delay indefinitely in following God.
options.note: The opposite: Joshua rebukes delay and urges them to act now.

options.text: God had failed to provide enough land.
options.note: God had fully provided; the failure was the tribes' slackness, not God's provision.

questions: Joshua asked, how long will you put off possessing what God has given you? Where in your life are you being slack about laying hold of something God has already provided?
The land was a sure gift, yet it still had to be entered. What blessings secured for you in Christ do you need to actively lay hold of rather than leave unclaimed?
The distribution was done by lot in the presence of the LORD, joining practical work to worship. How can you bring your ordinary decisions and work more consciously before God?
The Tent of Meeting was set up at the center of the nation. Is God's presence truly at the center of your life and priorities, or pushed to the edges?
Benjamin was small but strategically placed, holding key sites for God's purposes. How does it encourage you that God uses the small and seemingly insignificant for His plans?

translationNotes.note: The Tent of Meeting set up at Shiloh marks Israel's central sanctuary for the period of the judges, until the ark was taken in the days of Eli, 1 Samuel 4.
Jebus, that is, Jerusalem, lay on Benjamin's border; the BSB footnotes note variant readings for several names in this verse. The city would not be fully taken until David, 2 Samuel 5.
